claims.text: The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy is an ordered, single-phase hexagonal material.
Low-fluence Ar+ irradiation introduces a controlled and uniform density of point defects into the alloy.
The irradiation-induced point defects act as homogeneous nucleation centers during the magnetostructural transition.
Irradiation-induced point defects reduce local barriers to phase nucleation.
Reducing local nucleation barriers produces more spatially uniform phase propagation.
More spatially uniform phase propagation broadens and smooths the magnetostructural transition.
The defect-mediated change in nucleation and phase propagation reduces hysteresis during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
The irradiated alloy retains a significant magnetic entropy change under low applied fields.
The controlled intervention uses approximately 1×10^14 ions/cm² of 100 keV Ar+ irradiation under vacuum at room temperature.
The specified irradiation conditions produce point defects over a depth of a few hundred nanometers.
The specified irradiation conditions do not alter the bulk ordered phase.
Relative to an unirradiated control, irradiation produces a broader and less abrupt magnetocaloric transition.
Relative to an unirradiated control, irradiation reduces hysteretic losses.
Transition broadening is more pronounced in the irradiation-modified surface region than in the bulk.
The unirradiated as-deposited alloy has a sharp first-order magnetostructural transition.
The unirradiated as-deposited alloy has significant hysteresis.
The unirradiated as-deposited alloy exhibits entropy change over a limited temperature range.
Increasing fluence beyond a calibrated threshold risks excessive irradiation damage and invalidates the prediction.
A nonuniform defect distribution may cause deviations from the predicted response.
The magnitude of transition broadening and hysteresis reduction depends on the achieved defect density.
